title: Korean Coasts Part II: A Bicycle Journey Through Identity & Landscape – Molly Sugar
content:
Molly Sugar shares excerpts from her Korean Coasts zine, exploring identity, belonging, and landscape as a Korean adoptee. The second chapter of her bicycle journey through Korea follows two very different rides: a solo bike tour along Korea’s East Coast and a group ride around Jeju Island with friends.

Returning

I have only spent a tiny fraction of my life in South Korea. I was adopted and brought to the United States when I was three months old, and for much of my life Korea existed more as an idea than a place I truly knew. How do you make up for lost time?

The reality is that you probably can’t, and I have come to accept that. What I do know is that I want to spend more time in my motherland and soak up as much as I can whenever I am there. For me, bicycle touring is the perfect way to experience a place. It allows me to move slowly through the landscape, meet people, eat local food, and process what it means to be an adoptee returning to the country where I was born.

I have now returned to Korea three times, and each visit has marked a different chapter in my life.

My first trip back as an adult was in my early twenties. I visited with former college roommates, one of whom was teaching English in Korea. We stayed out too late at clubs and noraebangs 노래방 (karaoke), checked off tourist sites like the DMZ and the National Palace, and ate as much incredible Korean food as possible. It was a fun introduction, but I left feeling like there was still so much more to understand.

By my second visit, in my mid-thirties, I knew I wanted to experience Korea by bike. Cycling has shaped much of my life, and it felt like the most natural way to explore my connection to the country. In the fall of 2024, I rode from Seoul to Busan with two friends, including a fellow Korean adoptee. The journey changed me. It deepened my connection to Korea and showed me how powerful a bicycle can be as a tool for exploration, reflection, and belonging. You can read more about that experience in Seoul to Busan: Part One. As soon as the trip ended, I knew I wanted to return.

For this third visit, I wanted something different. I wanted to experience Korea both alone and in community. I wanted to see new landscapes, eat new foods, and meet people in different corners of the country. So I chose two very different rides: a solo journey along Korea’s East Coast and a group ride around Jeju Island with friends.

The two experiences could not have been more different, yet both felt necessary. The solitude of the East Coast gave me space to reflect, while Jeju brought connection, laughter, and shared memories. Together, they created a trip that filled my heart in ways I did not expect.

This zine is a reflection on both journeys. It is part practical guide for anyone interested in bicycle touring in Korea and part personal exploration of what it means to return to a homeland as an adoptee. It is about bikes, but it is also about much more than bikes. It is about the ways identity and landscape become intertwined, and how moving through a place by bike can create space to heal, reconnect, and better understand where you come from.

East Coast

Korea’s East Coast Bike Route is a stunning coastal journey stretching roughly 300 miles between the northern border region near the DMZ and the city of Ulsan in the south.

Along the way, riders are treated to dramatic ocean views, quiet fishing villages, fresh seafood, and some of the most beautiful stretches of coastline in the country. Compared to Korea’s inland cycling routes, the East Coast is hillier and requires sharing more roads with cars, but the scenery makes every climb worthwhile.

The route is typically ridden northbound to take advantage of prevailing winds, but I rode it southbound and never felt like the wind was working against me. To reach the coast, I took an express bus from Seoul to Sokcho, where it was easy to store my bike underneath the bus. After spending the night in Sokcho, I rode north to the entrance of the Unification Observatory and then returned to town. This is the northernmost point you can reach by bike, as access to the actual observatory near the DMZ requires additional transportation by bus.

That northernmost section ended up being one of my favorite sections of the entire trip. The route felt surprisingly remote, winding through farmland and stretches of overgrown bike path. It was quiet in a way that I had not expected, and it gave me time to settle into the rhythm of traveling alone.

Most of the route passes through small beach communities, with cities like Gangneung and Donghae appearing every other day. Unlike the highly isolated and mostly car-free Cross-Country Path, the East Coast route frequently shares roads with local traffic. That said, I was pleasantly surprised by how many dedicated bike paths followed the shoreline. Some of my favorite stretches hugged the ocean for miles, offering uninterrupted views of the sea.

I ended my ride in Pohang, where it was easy to catch a bus to Busan. The bus system is incredibly convenient and offers several drop off locations throughout the city. Locals told me that the section between Pohang and Busan tends to be the busiest and least enjoyable part of the route due to heavier traffic, so I decided to skip it entirely without any regrets.

I rode the East Coast in late October, and the conditions could not have been better. After delaying my departure a few days to avoid heavy rain, I was rewarded with cool temperatures, clear skies, and comfortable riding weather. Spring and fall are generally the best seasons for cycling in Korea. Summer brings crowds to the beaches, while winter can be quite cold and windy along the coast.

If you love ocean views, colorful fishing harbors, seaside bike paths, fresh seafood, and small towns that seem untouched by time, the East Coast route is hard to beat. Along the way you’ll pass giant king crab statues, traditional wooden pavilions overlooking the sea, picturesque lighthouses, trendy surf shacks, and dramatic rocky shorelines. Just be prepared for the constant rhythm of the coast: up a hill, down a hill, and then right back up another one. The views are worth every pedal stroke.

Jeju Island

The Jeju Fantasy Bicycle Path truly lives up to its name. Circling the entire island for roughly 150 miles, the route offers stunning coastal views, volcanic landscapes, and some of the most scenic riding in Korea.

Compared to the East Coast and the inland Cross-Country Path, Jeju is generally flatter, with gentle rolling hills that make it one of the most approachable long distance bike routes in the country. Known as the Hawaii of Korea, Jeju is South Korea’s premier island getaway. Its mild climate, dramatic volcanic terrain, waterfalls, lava caves, and unique cultural traditions attract visitors from across the country and around the world. Because of its popularity, Jeju was also the busiest cycling route I rode in Korea.

After spending days riding solo along the East Coast, arriving in Jeju felt like stepping into a completely different experience. Instead of long stretches of solitude, I was riding with friends and surrounded by people. We saw more cyclists here than anywhere else, including several solo women travelers, which was especially exciting since I was the only solo woman cyclist on the East Coast.

What made Jeju special for me was not just the riding, but the opportunity to share it with friends. As much as I value solo travel, there was something refreshing about experiencing Korea in community. We spent our days riding the coastline and our evenings exploring together, visiting places like the Haenyeo Museum, learning about Jeju’s famous women divers, and even making a stop at the quirky Sex Museum. Many of Jeju’s meals are designed to be shared family style, so having friends along also meant I could enjoy dishes that would have been difficult to order alone.

While there are a few stretches of dedicated bike path, most of the route follows local roads shared with cars. Fortunately, drivers were generally patient and respectful, and I never felt uncomfortable riding alongside traffic. The eastern side of the island offers some quieter and more remote sections, which ended up being my favorite parts of the route.

We rode the island in the recommended counterclockwise direction, keeping the ocean on our right and taking advantage of the prevailing winds. To get there, we flew from Busan to Jeju and later from Jeju to Seoul. Flights take about an hour and are relatively affordable. Since we rented bikes on the island, we did not have to worry about flying with our own bikes, which made travel much simpler.

We rode Jeju in early November and were treated to mostly sunny skies and temperatures in the mid 60s. We did have one day of relentless rain and headwinds, which made me grateful it was the exception rather than the rule. While Jeju stays slightly warmer than the mainland, summers can be extremely humid and bring monsoon rains. Spring and fall are generally the best times to ride. Because the route is relatively flat, the island’s famous coastal winds are often the biggest challenge.

If you love beautiful coastlines, matriarchal cultural history, waterfalls, lava caves, and vibrant seaside towns, Jeju is hard to beat. Along the way you’ll pass sculptures honoring the Haenyeo women divers, wind farms, citrus farms, endless rows of drying squid, black volcanic cliffs, and countless ocean views. It is a route that feels both relaxed and adventurous, and one that is best enjoyed at a pace slow enough to take it all in.

Alone & Together

Before this trip, I had never bike toured alone for multiple days, let alone in another country. The idea of spending seven days riding solo along Korea’s East Coast felt both exciting and slightly intimidating.

As a Korean adoptee returning to my motherland, there was also an emotional side to traveling alone. Every day brought new experiences, unfamiliar places, and moments that stirred up feelings I wasn’t always expecting. Some days I felt deeply connected to Korea. Other days I felt like an outsider looking in.

There is something powerful about moving through the landscape of your birth country under your own power. Unlike visiting cities or checking off tourist attractions, cycling allows you to experience the spaces in between. The small towns, the farms, the roadside restaurants, and the everyday moments that most visitors pass by. Riding gave me the time and space to connect with Korea at a slower pace and reflect on my relationship to a place that feels both familiar and unfamiliar at the same time.

Traveling alone also meant there was nowhere to hide from my thoughts. Some days that felt challenging. Other days it felt like a gift. The long stretches of coastline, the rhythm of pedaling, and the quiet moments at the end of the day created space to process emotions that often get drowned out by the busyness of everyday life.

Then came Jeju.

After a week of solitude, arriving on Jeju Island with friends felt like stepping into a different version of the same journey. The landscapes were beautiful, but what stood out most was the sense of connection. Instead of spending my days alone with my thoughts, I spent them sharing meals, conversations, and experiences with people who understood why this trip mattered.

My friend Mai-li is also a Korean adoptee, and we had ridden Korea’s Cross-Country Path together the year before. My friend Sara’s mom is a Korean adoptee, and this was Sara’s first trip to Korea. In different ways, all three of us were navigating questions of identity, belonging, and what it meant to be in Korea.

We talked openly about the strange experience of feeling Korean but not fully Korean. Of being connected to a place while also feeling disconnected from it. Of wanting to learn more about our histories while trying to stay present and appreciate the experience in front of us. These conversations often happened while riding side by side, over shared meals, or during quiet moments at the end of the day.

The East Coast and Jeju offered two very different experiences, but I came to realize that I needed both. The solo ride gave me space for reflection, while Jeju reminded me of the importance of community. One helped me listen inward. The other helped me feel understood.
As adoptees, so much of our journey can feel solitary. This trip reminded me that it doesn’t always have to be. Sometimes the most meaningful part of returning is having people beside you who understand the questions you’re carrying, even if none of you have the answers.

Closing Reflections

One of my favorite moments on the East Coast happened after a particularly steep climb. Tired and grinding my way uphill, I finally reached the top and was rewarded with my favorite part of cycling: the descent.

As I flew down the steepest hill of the entire trip, I spotted a group of older women, ajummas, gathered at the bottom. As I passed, they started cheering and clapping for me. It was a small, unexpected moment, but one that has stayed with me long after the trip ended.
At that exact moment, I was listening to “Little Balcony” by Hyukoh and Sunset Rollercoaster:

You’re gone
Forever young
Eternal sun
Go have some fun
Don’t get me wrong
I love you so much
I’m glad you stop
Your endless run

The lyrics almost sound like a gentle voice saying: “You don’t have to keep running. You’re here. Enjoy this moment.” Something about the music, the cheering strangers, and the feeling of flying down that hill came together in a way that felt impossible to recreate. It was one of those fleeting travel moments that becomes larger in memory than it seemed at the time.

Riding alone on the East Coast and with friends on Jeju Island reminded me that I needed both experiences to fully embrace this return to Korea. The East Coast gave me space for solitude and reflection. Jeju brought connection, laughter, and community. Together, they created a journey that felt complete.

As adoptees, we often talk about searching for connection, belonging, or pieces of ourselves. Sometimes that search looks dramatic, but more often it happens in small moments: eating convenience store ramyeon after a long day of riding, watching the ocean waves from a harbor, reflecting on a funny conversation with a friend, or being cheered on by a group of ajummas at the bottom of a hill. Those moments became just as meaningful as the miles themselves.

I have only spent a small fraction of my life in Korea, but each visit deepens my connection to the place in ways I never expect. I know I can never make up for lost time, but I hope to keep returning. To discover more, learn more, and continue building my relationship with my motherland, one bike trip at a time.

If this zine resonated with you, consider supporting BIPOC Adoptees, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to creating safe, inclusive spaces for adoptees of color. Their mission is to uplift BIPOC adoptees through community, storytelling, education, and care, while challenging the systemic erasure and neglect adoptees often experience.
